content.text: Gandhian Philosophy and Mass Satyagrahas, Subhas Chandra Bose and the INA, Sardar Patel and Territorial Integration, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar and the Constitution, and Linguistic States Reorganization

The climactic epoch of the Indian national movement and its post-independence consolidation was shaped by ideological dynamism and statecraft: Mahatma Gandhi's philosophy of non-violent mass satyagraha, Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose's militant anti-imperial struggle through the Indian National Army (INA), Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel's integration of 565 princely states, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar's egalitarian constitutional architecture, and the linguistic reorganization of states originating in Andhra.

content.text: 1. Mahatma Gandhi: Philosophical Tenets & Pan-Indian Satyagrahas

content.caption: Core Tenets of Gandhian Philosophy and Landmark Mass Satyagrahas
rows: Satyagraha & Ahimsa
Soul-force (truth-force) grounded in active, unyielding non-violence (Ahimsa); holding on to Truth (Satya) while suffering without malice toward the oppressor.
Transformed the Indian national movement from elite petitioning into an unstoppable multi-class mass movement engaging peasants, workers, and women.
Sarvodaya & Trusteeship
Upliftment of all (Sarvodaya based on John Ruskin's 'Unto This Last'); capitalists should consider wealth as trustees for the welfare of the poorest (Daridranarayana).
Decentralized village republics (Gram Swaraj); promotion of Khadi and village cottage industries as instruments of economic self-sufficiency.
Early Local Experiments (1917–1918)

Champaran (1917, Bihar: Tinkathia indigo system), Ahmedabad Mill Strike (1918, Gujarat: first hunger strike for 35% wage hike), Kheda (1918, Gujarat: first non-cooperation against revenue extraction during crop failure).
Established Gandhi's technique of localized direct action; allied with Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, Rajendra Prasad, and J.B. Kripalani.
Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–1922)
Launched post-Rowlatt Act, Jallianwala Bagh massacre (13 April 1919), and Khilafat issue.
Boycott of government schools, law courts, foreign cloth, and titles; suspended abruptly following the Chauri Chaura incident (5 February 1922) where 22 policemen were burned alive.
Civil Disobedience Movement (1930–1934)
Inaugurated by the Dandi March (12 March – 6 April 1930; 240 miles from Sabarmati to Dandi with 78 chosen followers) breaking the colonial Salt Law.
Salt became universal symbol of defiance; mass picketing; Dharasana salt raid led by Sarojini Naidu; Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931); Gandhi attended Second Round Table Conference in London.
Quit India Movement (August 1942)
Historic AICC session at Gowalia Tank, Bombay (8 August 1942); Gandhi's clarion call 'Do or Die' (Karo ya Maro).
Top leaders arrested overnight; leaderless mass rebellion; parallel governments (Jatiya Sarkar in Tamluk, Prati Sarkar in Satara under Nana Patil, Ballia under Chittu Pandey).

content.text: 2. Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose & The Indian National Army (INA)

items: Ideological Rift with Gandhi: Bose advocated uncompromising radical militancy and industrial planning (chaired National Planning Committee 1938); elected Congress President at Haripura (1938) and Tripuri (1939, defeating Gandhi's candidate Pattabhi Sitaramayya); resigned to form the Forward Bloc.

Great Escape to Axis Powers (1941): Escaped house arrest in Calcutta; traveled via Kabul and Moscow to Berlin (met Hitler; formed the Indian Legion); traveled by submarine (U-180 and I-29) to Tokyo in 1943.

Revival of the Indian National Army (Azad Hind Fauj): Originally formed by Mohan Singh with Indian PoWs; Bose assumed supreme command in Singapore (July 1943); proclaimed the Provisional Government of Free India (Arzi Hukumat-e-Azad Hind) on 21 October 1943; recognized by Axis powers; issued slogans 'Give me blood, and I will give you freedom' and 'Dilli Chalo'.
Rani of Jhansi Regiment: Formed Asia's first all-female combat military unit under Captain Lakshmi Sahgal.
Imphal and Kohima Campaigns: INA fought alongside Japanese forces on the Burma-Manipur border; hoisted the national tricolor at Moirang, Manipur (April 1944).

INA Trials at Red Fort (1945–1946): Joint trial of Prem Sahgal, Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon, and Shahnawaz Khan ignited nationwide mutinies across the Royal Indian Navy (RIN Revolt in Bombay, February 1946), hastening the British decision to quit India.

content.text: 3. Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel & The Territorial Integration of India

content.caption: Integration of Princely States under Sardar Patel and V.P. Menon
rows: Accession Architecture
565 Princely States given option under Indian Independence Act 1947 to join India, Pakistan, or remain independent.
Patel utilized a combination of patriotic persuasion, privy purses, and the threat of force; signed Instrument of Accession on Defence, External Affairs, and Communications.
Junagadh (Gujarat)
Nawab Muhammad Mahabat Khanji declared accession to Pakistan despite having an 80%+ Hindu population and no land contiguity.
Citizens established provisional government (Aarzi Hukumat); Nawab fled to Karachi; plebiscite conducted in February 1948 voted 99%+ in favor of merging with India.
Hyderabad (Deccan)
Nizam Mir Osman Ali Khan declared independence, funded communal Razakar militia under Kasim Razvi committing atrocities against rural peasants.
Operation Polo (Police Action, 13–17 September 1948): Indian Army commanded by Major General J.N. Chaudhuri marched into Hyderabad; Nizam surrendered and acceded to the Indian Union.
Kashmir
Maharaja Hari Singh signed Standstill Agreement; Pakistan launched armed tribal invasion (Operation Gulmarg) in October 1947.
Maharaja signed Instrument of Accession on 26 October 1947; Indian Army airlifted to Srinagar, expelling invaders from Kashmir Valley.

content.text: 4. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar: Social Justice & Constitutional Architecture

content.caption: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, Chairman of the Drafting Committee, presenting the final draft of the Indian Constitution to President Dr. Rajendra Prasad on 25 November 1949.
content.alt_text: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar presenting Constitution to Dr. Rajendra Prasad

items: Social Justice Movements: Mahad Satyagraha (1927) asserting the civic right of untouchables to drink water from the public Chawdar tank; publicly burned the Manusmriti (25 December 1927); Kalaram Temple entry satyagraha (1930) at Nashik; founded Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha (1924) with the slogan 'Educate, Agitate, Organise'.

Poona Pact (24 September 1932): Signed between Ambedkar and Madan Mohan Malaviya (representing Gandhi on fast unto death in Yerwada Jail) rejecting Ramsay MacDonald's Communal Award of separate electorates for Depressed Classes; secured reserved seats increased from 71 to 148 in provincial legislatures under joint electorates.

Father of the Indian Constitution: Appointed Chairman of the 7-member Drafting Committee on 29 August 1947; embedded Fundamental Rights (Part III), abolition of untouchability (Article 17), Right to Constitutional Remedies as 'Heart and Soul' of the Constitution (Article 32), and affirmative action reservations.

First Law Minister & Hindu Code Bill: Resigned from the Cabinet in 1951 over conservative resistance to the progressive Hindu Code Bill (championing divorce rights, women's property inheritance, and monogamy); embraced Buddhism along with half a million followers at Deekshabhoomi, Nagpur on 14 October 1956.

content.text: 5. Linguistic Reorganization of States & Creation of Andhra State

content.caption: Chronology of States Reorganization in Post-Independence India
rows: S.K. Dhar Commission
June 1948
Appointed by Constituent Assembly; rejected linguistic basis; recommended reorganization purely on administrative convenience, financial viability, and geography.
JVP Committee (Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel, Pattabhi Sitaramayya)
December 1948
Submitted report in 1949; rejected linguistic states in the national interest, but conceded that special consideration could be given if public sentiment was overwhelmingly unified.
Potti Sreeramulu's Epic Fast & Formation of Andhra State
October–December 1952

Potti Sreeramulu undertook an indefinite hunger strike in Madras demanding a separate Telugu-speaking state; attained martyrdom after 58 days on 15 December 1952; triggered massive civil unrest; Prime Minister Nehru announced creation of Andhra State on 1 October 1953 (capital at Kurnool, High Court at Guntur) as the FIRST linguistic state in India.
States Reorganisation Commission (SRC / Fazal Ali Commission)

Headed by Justice Fazal Ali, with members K.M. Panikkar and H.N. Kunzru; recommended redrawing state boundaries on linguistic lines while preserving national unity; rejected 'one language, one state' dogma.

Resulted in States Reorganisation Act 1956 (7th Constitutional Amendment), creating 14 States and 6 Union Territories. Unified Andhra State with Telangana (Gentlemen's Agreement) to form unified Andhra Pradesh on 1 November 1956.

content.text: Part A: Mains Analytical & Descriptive Questions

items:
Compare and contrast the political philosophies, methods of resistance, and visions for independent India of Mahatma Gandhi and Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose. (APPSC Group-1 Mains, 10 Marks)
-> Model Approach: Detail areas of common ground: unshakeable devotion to swaraj, mutual respect (Bose was first to call Gandhi 'Father of the Nation' in 1944; Gandhi hailed Bose as the 'Patriot of Patriots'); analyze fundamental philosophical divergences: Means vs Ends (Gandhi held that impure violent means corrupt pure ends; Bose believed ethical absolute pacifism could not dislodge a ruthless colonial empire, embracing international realpolitik alliances with Axis powers); Vision of Economy: Gandhi advocated decentralized village republics, cottage Khadi, and minimal industrialization; Bose advocated rapid socialist industrialization, state central planning, and heavy machines; evaluate their complementary roles in achieving independence.

Evaluate the monumental role of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel in the territorial and political consolidation of post-independence India. How did he resolve the accession crises in Junagadh, Hyderabad, and Kashmir? (APPSC Group-1 Mains, 10 Marks)
-> Model Approach: Outline the catastrophic threat of 'Balkanization' posed by the lapse of paramountcy over 565 princely states; evaluate Patel's pragmatic carrot-and-stick strategy assisted by V.P. Menon: appeals to patriotism, guarantee of privy purses, and deployment of coercive state power; detail the resolution of Junagadh (Aarzi Hukumat, plebiscite), Hyderabad (defiance of the Nizam and Razakars, decisive military intervention via Operation Polo in September 1948), and Kashmir (expulsion of Pakistani tribal raiders following the Instrument of Accession); conclude on his enduring legacy as the 'Iron Man of India'.

Trace the historic agitation led by Potti Sreeramulu for the formation of Andhra State. How did his supreme sacrifice catalyze the linguistic reorganization of states throughout India? (APPSC Group-1 Mains, 10 Marks)
-> Model Approach: Detail the historical demand of the Andhra Mahasabha since 1913 for separation from the multilingual Madras Presidency; analyze the stalling reports of the Dhar Commission and JVP Committee prioritizing administrative unity over language; describe Potti Sreeramulu's 58-day fast unto death starting 19 October 1952 at Bulusu Sambamurti's house in Madras; analyze the volcanic popular fury following his martyrdom on 15 December 1952; explain Nehru's announcement creating Andhra State on 1 October 1953 as the first linguistic state; evaluate the domino effect compelling the appointment of the Fazal Ali Commission (SRC 1953) and the nationwide redrawing of India's political map on linguistic lines in 1956.

content.text: Part B: Screening / Prelims Objective Questions

items:
Q1. Amarajeevi Potti Sreeramulu attained martyrdom on 15 December 1952 following a historic fast-unto-death lasting how many days?
(a) 45 days
(b) 52 days
(c) 58 days
(d) 63 days
Correct Answer: (c) 58 days [Explanation: Potti Sreeramulu began his fast on 19 October 1952 and breathed his last on 15 December 1952, enduring an epic hunger strike of 58 days for a separate Andhra state.]

Q2. The military police action launched by the Indian Army in September 1948 to integrate the princely state of Hyderabad into the Indian Union was code-named:
(a) Operation Vijay
(b) Operation Polo
(c) Operation Cactus
(d) Operation Blue Star
Correct Answer: (b) Operation Polo [Explanation: Operation Polo was the code name of the military action launched on 13 September 1948 that liberated Hyderabad and integrated it into the Indian Union.]

Q3. The historic Poona Pact of September 1932 was signed between Dr. B.R. Ambedkar and which nationalist leader on behalf of caste Hindus?
(a) Mahatma Gandhi
(b) Madan Mohan Malaviya
(c) Jawaharlal Nehru
(d) Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel
Correct Answer: (b) Madan Mohan Malaviya [Explanation: Because Mahatma Gandhi was observing an indefinite fast in Yerwada Jail, Pandit Madan Mohan Malaviya signed the Poona Pact on behalf of caste Hindus alongside Dr. B.R. Ambedkar.]

Q4. Which famous slogan was proclaimed by Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose upon assuming supreme leadership of the Indian National Army (INA) in Singapore in 1943?
(a) Inquilab Zindabad
(b) Dilli Chalo
(c) Jai Jawan Jai Kisan
(d) Vande Mataram
Correct Answer: (b) Dilli Chalo [Explanation: Netaji gave the historic battle cry 'Dilli Chalo' (March to Delhi) to inspire the soldiers of the Azad Hind Fauj in July 1943.]

Q5. Which constitutional amendment enacted the recommendations of the States Reorganisation Commission (Fazal Ali Commission) in 1956, abolishing Part A, B, C, and D states?
(a) 1st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951
(b) 7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956
(c) 14th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1962
(d) 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976
Correct Answer: (b) 7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956 [Explanation: The 7th Amendment Act, 1956 gave constitutional effect to the States Reorganisation scheme, establishing 14 states and 6 union territories.]
